report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .07", Sentence = "Overt victimization trended toward statistical significance (p = .07), with greater experiences of overt victimization corresponding to higher reports of social anxiety."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Adolescence is a developmental period characterized by increased interest in peer relationships and social inclusion.
Rejection sensitivity (RS) -the tendency to anticipate, perceive, and experience heightened emotional responses to rejection -is common in adolescence and linked to internalizing symptoms.
However, RS is understudied in autistic adolescents despite their social communication differences, increased risk of peer rejection, and online lived experiences of heightened rejection sensitivity.
It is also unknown how RS impacts different mental health symptoms and whether it might contribute to the heightened prevalence of anxiety and depression in autistic youth.
In the present study, 106 autistic adolescents (14-17 years old) completed surveys of RS, internalizing symptoms, autistic traits, self-esteem, and peer victimization.
Results showed that virtually all autistic adolescents experienced a degree of RS, with higher rates among females and those with higher autistic traits.

Hierarchical regression models indicated that Anxious RS predicted social anxiety symptoms above and beyond traditional risk and protective factors, but neither Anxious nor Angry RS predicted depression or generalized anxiety.

Findings have implications for risk stratification models and point to potential intervention targets; yet more research is needed to determine the directionality of relationships with rejection sensitivity.

In this study, researchers recruited 106 autistic teenagers (14-17 years old) to complete surveys which measured RS, depression and anxiety, autistic traits, self-esteem, and victimization experiences.
Researchers found that all autistic teenagers experienced some level of RS, and that being female and having higher autistic traits were associated with higher RS.
Anxious RS was linked with higher social anxiety symptoms, even above and beyond other risk factors, such as low self-esteem and bullying experiences.
However, RS was not associated with increased depression or generalized anxiety symptoms when taking other factors into consideration.
More work should be done to see if autistic teenagers have higher rejection sensitivity than non-autistic teenagers, and to further explore its potential effect on mental health.

text.text: In the face of more ambiguous social situations and cues, individuals with higher RS may expect to be rejected or assume rejection occurred, resulting in negative emotional and behavioral responses.
Internalizing responses to rejection, such as nervousness, are known as anxious RS, while externalizing responses, such as irritability, are known as angry RS (Downey et al., 1998).

The RS model describes a negative feedback loop, with new rejection experiences contributing to additional learned fears of rejection, effectively increasing sensitivity.

Although social rejection can be distressing for adolescents, autistic adolescents may be disproportionally affected by social rejection.

Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by differences in social communication, including in social reciprocity, social interactions, and in forming and maintaining relationships (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).

These characteristics are accompanied by repetitive behaviors (e.g., repetitive motor movements) and sensory sensitivities (i.e., negative responses to environmental stimuli) that appear early in development.

Given these differences, unfortunately, autistic adolescents experience greater peer rejection and victimization relative to their non-autistic peers, often in response to social miscommunications (Daghustani et al., 2025; Sreckovic et al., 2014).

text.text: Taken together, autistic adolescents value social belonging and peer acceptance, yet they face both unique barriers to peer acceptance and an elevated risk of rejection, which may make them particularly susceptible to the negative mental health consequences of rejection experiences.

The present study seeks to extend research on RS to autistic adolescents, better understand the lived experiences of autistic teens, and identify if RS presents a unique vulnerability to mental health problems in this population.
Specifically, we aimed to: (1) characterize RS in a community sample of autistic adolescents, and (2) examine RS as a predictor of internalizing symptoms.

Given the well-documented lived experiences of autistic people facing heightened RS, it was hypothesized that RS would be prevalent in autistic adolescents and would contribute significantly to depression, generalized anxiety, and social anxiety.
The sample included 106 autistic adolescents without intellectual disability.
Participants ranged in age from 14 to 17 years old (M = 15.3) and were 68% male.
The sample was mostly White (59%) and approximately half identified as Hispanic/Latino (48.5%).

All participants were diagnosed with autism through a prior evaluation or an evaluation provided through the study; The present study is a secondary data analysis of cross-sectional data collected from adolescent self-report at the baseline timepoint.
At baseline, adolescents completed several surveys assessing their RS profile, internalizing symptoms, autistic traits, peer victimization experiences, and self-esteem.
Families received monetary compensation and a free psychological assessment report (if desired) for their participation.
Adolescent rejection sensitivity (RS) was measured using the Children's Rejection Sensitivity Questionnaire (CRSQ; Downey et al., 1998).

text.text: The measure presented adolescents with 12 social scenarios with ambiguous social rejection cues and instructed participants to imagine themselves in each situation described.
For example, one item asks, "Imagine you're back in your classroom‚ and everyone is splitting up into groups to work on a special project together.
You sit there and watch lots of other kids getting picked.
As you wait‚ you wonder if the kids will want you for their group."

Participants then responded to three questions for each of the 12 social situations: (1) how nervous they would be in this situation (i.e., anxious RS), (2) how mad they would be in this situation (i.e., angry RS), and ( 3) to what extent they expect the rejection to happen (i.e., expectancy).

text.text: Participants numerically rated how nervous and mad they would feel in each situation on a 6-point scale [e.g., 'not nervous/not mad' (=1) to 'very nervous/very mad' (=6)].
Adolescents rated their expectancy of being rejected on a scale of 'no' (=1) to 'yes' (=6).
Due to the wording of certain scenarios, expectancy scores on items 2 and 12 were reversecoded.
Anxious and Angry RS scores were computed by multiplying the anxiety score with the expectancy score, and the anger score with the expectancy score, respectively.
This process was repeated for each scenario and then averaged across the Anxious items and Angry items; a total score was not produced and instead, two separate scores of Anxious and Angry RS.
Possible scores ranged from 1 to 36 in both the anxious and angry rejection sensitivity domains, with higher scores indicating greater RS.
Internal consistency was acceptable for both anxious RS (α = .86) and angry RS (α = .82).
Of note, the research team created a set of visual aids to ease the administration of the CRSQ and to facilitate comprehension for participants.
Visual aids were developed for the 12 social situations and for each of the nervous, mad, and expectancy rating scales (see Supplemental Materials).
The visual aids were presented to each participant with the verbal instructions for each scenario and participants were invited to provide their ratings verbally or by pointing.

Peer victimization experiences were measured using the Overt and Relational Victimization in Adolescents (ORAA), a self-report questionnaire of the frequency of various forms of peer victimization.
Response options for each item range from "Never" to "A few times a week."

Scores for overt and relational victimization were summed across items, with possible scores ranging from 4 (overt) and 5 (relational), to 20 (overt) and 25 (relational).

text.text: All participants reported some degree of rejection sensitivity, and on average, anxious RS was higher than angry RS.

Anxious RS was positively correlated with depressive symptoms, generalized anxiety symptoms, and social anxiety symptoms such that individuals with higher anxious RS also reported higher internalizing symptoms.

Additionally, anxious RS was positively related to angry RS, autistic traits, and overt and relational victimization such that individuals with higher anxious RS also reported higher angry RS, autistic traits, and more frequent victimization.

Prior research shows autistic adolescents are at a greater risk of peer rejection and internalizing disorders compared to non-autistic adolescents (Chandler et al., 2016; Gurbuz et al., 2024; Lai et al., 2019; Sreckovic et al., 2014); however, there is limited research on the experience of RS in this population, despite discussions of lived experiences of heightened RS within autistic communities (Van Asselt et al., 2025).

text.text: To our knowledge, the present study is the first to identify correlates of RS and examine cross-sectional associations with internalizing symptoms in a sample of autistic adolescents.
Our findings not only emphasize the importance of RS on mental health outcomes in this population, but also empirically support the lived experiences of autistic people.
Virtually all autistic adolescents experienced a degree of RS.

On average, autistic adolescents reported greater anxious RS than angry RS, suggesting that they are more likely to anxiously anticipate and expect rejection in ambiguous situations than respond angrily.

One possible explanation of greater anxious RS in this population could be that internalizing disorders (i.e., anxiety disorders) are one of the most common mental health conditions experienced by autistic people (Hossain et al., 2020; Postorino et al., 2023; Van Steensel et al., 2011); longitudinal studies are needed to understand to what extent RS may contribute to internalizing disorders, and vice versa, in this population.

text.text: Taken together, elevated rates of RS and internalizing behavioral reactions in this population highlights the importance of rejection sensitivity as a point of treatment intervention.
Sex assigned at birth was significantly associated with both types of RS, with autistic females experiencing greater anxious and angry RS than autistic males.
The literature on sex differences of adolescent RS in the general population is both limited and mixed.
In non-autistic samples, Marston et al. (2010) found that RS is greater in males during late adolescence, while Giovazolias (2023) found significantly higher anxious RS in female adolescents.

text.text: Elevated RS in autistic females could be attributed to sex differences in social camouflaging (i.e., masking) in autistic youth as several studies have shown that female autistic youth engage in more camouflaging behaviors than males, a strategy used to suppress and compensate for autistic behaviors to appear non-autistic (Dean et al., 2017; Simcoe et al., 2018; Tubío-Fungueiriño et al., 2021).

text.text: Since camouflaging behaviors require identifying traits in oneself that deviate from the "social norm" and modifying them with the intent to be more socially accepted, it is possible that autistic females are more hypervigilant of their behaviors and more expectant of rejection in social situations, contributing to increased RS.

More broadly, research also shows that adolescent girls experience greater concerns regarding peer acceptance and rejection than boys (Henrich et al., 2001; Liu & Kaplan, 1999; McLean & Anderson, 2009), which may contribute to higher levels of RS.

text.text: In aggregate, it is possible that autistic female adolescents experience greater hypervigilance about their conformity to social situations and may mask to avoid rejection, contributing to apprehension about peer rejection and therefore greater RS.
Longitudinal studies are needed to test these potential explanations and interactions.
The present study also established that autistic teenagers with more autistic traits also reported a greater degree of both anxious and angry RS.
This is consistent with previous work suggesting that greater autistic traits heightened sensitivity to rejection in a general adult population without formal autism diagnoses (Lin et al., 2022).

text.text: Much like sex differences, the literature on autistic traits and RS is both sparse and mixed, and, to our knowledge, has not been examined in a sample of autistic adolescents prior to the present study.
Our findings extend knowledge of RS to a clinically-diagnosed autistic adolescent population, accounting for the unique social dynamics of having a clinically significant number of autistic traits.
Importantly, this study also explores the potential effects of RS on several mental health outcomes; namely depression, generalized anxiety, and social anxiety.

While anxious and angry RS did not appear to uniquely contribute to depression or generalized anxiety above and beyond more traditional risk and protective factors (e.g., self-esteem and peer victimization), anxious RS presented a unique risk for increased social anxiety.

This finding appears intuitive as social anxiety symptoms are characterized by a fear of negative social evaluations by other people (Leichsenring & Leweke, 2017; Morrison & Heimberg, 2013), which aligns with anxious RS processes.

text.text: It is important to note, however, that anxious RS and social anxiety are not synonymous constructs, as anxious RS represents a cognitive-affective vulnerability that may contribute to the development and cyclical maintenance of social anxiety symptoms.
This predictive association demonstrates that anxious RS captures a key variance in social anxiety beyond a fear of social interactions.

In summary, while RS may not be a key contributor to depression or generalized anxiety in this autistic adolescent sample, it may be an important treatment target for social anxiety in this population.
It is worth discussing that negative self-esteem was strongly, consistently associated with all adverse mental health outcomes.

This relation is well-documented in non-autistic populations (Downey & Feldman, 1996; Lei et al., 2024; Watson & Nesdale, 2012), and the present study suggests that high self-esteem may be protective against poor mental health for autistic adolescents in the same way.

text.text: Importantly, however, autistic youth tend to have lower self-esteem on average than their non-autistic counterparts, highlighting the unique vulnerabilities of this population to mental health problems (Cooper et al., 2017; McCauley et al., 2019; Van Der Cruijsen & Boyer, 2021) as well as potential promise for future treatment interventions.

text.text: Collectively, the present study's findings suggest that mental health in autistic adolescents is shaped by various risk and protective factors, and that anxious RS may be important for addressing social anxiety.
There are both strengths and limitations in the present study.

The primary strength is our exploration of RS in autistic adolescents from their perspectives, filling a large gap in the literature on autistic adolescents while empirically supporting the lived experiences of autistic people.

In addition to highlighting important clinical implications of RS for social anxiety, we also were able to identify that self-esteem should likely be addressed in tandem with RS to support the mental health of autistic youth.

Additionally, findings were based upon reports of autistic adolescents rather than caregiver reports, directly capturing their perspectives of their own internal experiences rather than relying on a proximal informant.

Lastly, the use of a community sample of autistic adolescents, as opposed to a sample recruited for comorbid internalizing disorders, strengthens the external validity of our findings to more autistic youth.
There are also limitations to the study.
First, our study is cross-sectional in design and therefore causal direction is unable to be defined.

Second, although it is a strength to include adolescents' personal reports of their feelings and experiences, self-report measures can be impacted by participants' level of insight into themselves, recall bias, and differences in respondent interpretations of questionnaires, among other biases.
Third, there is an absence of a comparison group of non-autistic adolescents, which limits the ability to determine if these findings are unique to autism.
Lastly, race and ethnicity were collapsed into binary groups for analytic purposes and thus, findings do not accurately reflect the diversity of lived experiences in this sample.
Future research should include a longitudinal design, a comparison group of nonautistic adolescents, and multimodal measurements of the concepts analyzed.

Nonetheless, considering the large empirical gap on the experiences and consequences of rejection sensitivity for autistic teens, our findings serve as an important foundation for future scientific work in this area.
The present study characterizes rejection sensitivity as a common, elevated experience for autistic adolescents that has potential implications for mental health.
In particular, it identifies a potential relation with social anxiety, and highlights other important risk and protective factors, such as sex assigned at birth and self-esteem.

Future longitudinal research is needed to establish the directionality of these associations, as well as the inclusion of non-autistic comparison samples to identify potential unique associations in autistic adolescents.
